text.headline: Introduction: The Warsaw Ghetto
text.text:
In October 1940, the German authorities ordered the establishment of a ghetto in Warsaw. Sealed the following month, it confined almost 30 percent of the city’s population within just 2.4 percent of its area. At its height, more than 400,000 Jews were imprisoned within its boundaries.

Mass deportations from the Warsaw Ghetto began in July 1942. In April 1943, those who remained launched an armed uprising. German forces suppressed the uprising and systematically burned and destroyed the ghetto; by May 1943, the area lay largely in ruins.

In the decades that followed, monuments, memorials and commemorative spaces transformed this landscape once again. 

This StoryMap follows the Hero’s Path through the former Warsaw Ghetto to explore not only the people and events it commemorates, but how the memory of the Warsaw Ghetto has been constructed over time and by whom.

media.caption: Memorial Route of Jewish Martyrdom and Struggle, commonly known as the Hero’s Path, at Zamenhofa and Anielewicza Streets.
media.credit: Photograph by Adrian Grycuk, 2013. Wikimedia Commons. CC BY-SA 3.0 PL
media.url: //uploads.knightlab.com/storymapjs/d186b003ea8a97a50c2408f0313b64c3/hero-s-path-warsaw-who-owns-memory/_images/Zamenhofa corner of Anielewicza Street in Warsaw.jpg

text.headline: Creating the Hero’s Path 1988
text.text:
On 18 April 1988, on the eve of the 45th anniversary of the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising, the Memorial Route of Jewish Martyrdom and Struggle commonly known as the Hero’s Path was unveiled in Warsaw. Designed by Zbigniew Gąsior, Stanisław Jankowski and Marek Moderau, the route connected sites associated with the Warsaw Ghetto, resistance and deportation.

The route is marked by black syenite stones bearing inscriptions in Polish and Hebrew. Through the people and places selected for commemoration, the Hero’s Path presents different forms of resistance and response: leadership and fighters of the uprising, spiritual and cultural resistance, and solidarity and help.

Beginning here, the route leads through the former ghetto toward the Umschlagplatz. As we follow it, we can ask not only who these individuals were, but why they were chosen for commemoration and what their selection tells us about how the Warsaw Ghetto was remembered in 1988.

media.caption: Emanuel Ringelblum, historian and founder of the clandestine Oyneg Shabes archive in the Warsaw Ghetto.
media.credit: Jewish Historical Institute

text.headline: Emanuel Ringelblum Preserving the Record
text.text:
Historian Emanuel Ringelblum understood that documenting what was happening to Warsaw’s Jews was itself an act of resistance. In the ghetto, he organised the clandestine Oyneg Shabes archive, bringing together writers, teachers, activists and ordinary residents to record their experiences under German occupation.

The group collected diaries, letters, photographs, underground newspapers, official notices and accounts of persecution and murder. As the destruction of the ghetto approached, members of the archive buried the material in metal boxes and milk cans. Two caches were recovered after the war; a third has never been found.

Ringelblum escaped from the ghetto and went into hiding with his wife, Judyta, and their son, Uri, in the “Krysia” bunker at 81 Grójecka Street. On 7 March 1944, the hiding place was discovered by the Germans. Ringelblum, his family, the other Jews hiding there and their Polish rescuers were arrested and subsequently murdered.

Ringelblum’s place on the Hero’s Path reminds us that resistance did not only take place with weapons. Recording events, preserving individual voices and ensuring that evidence would survive were also ways of resisting the attempt to erase Jewish lives and experiences.

media.caption: Józef Lewartowski (Aron Finkelstein), organiser of Jewish resistance in the Warsaw Ghetto and co-founder of the Anti-Fascist Bloc.
media.credit: Photographer unknown. Public domain. Source: Wikimedia Commons; originally reproduced by the Jewish Historical Institute. The Commons record traces the image to Bernard Mark's 1953 JHI publication and also identifies a Yad Vashem record (Item 73841).

text.headline: Józef Lewartowski Organising Resistance
text.text:
Józef Lewartowski was a communist political activist and one of the early organisers of armed Jewish resistance in the Warsaw Ghetto. In March 1942, he helped establish the Anti-Fascist Bloc, which brought together Communists and members of several Zionist and socialist groups in an attempt to organise resistance against the Germans.

The Anti-Fascist Bloc preceded the formation of the Jewish Fighting Organization (ŻOB) later that year. Its history reflects both the growing movement toward armed resistance and the political divisions within the ghetto. Jewish resistance in Warsaw was never represented by a single organisation.

Lewartowski was arrested during the mass deportations in the summer of 1942 and was shot in the ghetto in August.

His commemoration extends beyond the Hero’s Path. In 1958, a street in Warsaw was named for Lewartowski. Decades later, during Poland’s post-Communist decommunisation process, an attempt was made to rename the street for Marek Edelman. The decision was overturned by the courts, and Lewartowski’s name remained part of Warsaw’s landscape

text.headline: Michał Klepfisz  Preparing for Armed Resistance
text.text:
Michał Klepfisz was an engineer and a member of Tsukunft, the Bund’s youth movement. He later became active in the Bund’s underground organisation and joined the Jewish Fighting Organization (ŻOB).

As preparations for armed resistance developed, Klepfisz’s technical knowledge became particularly important. Through contact with the Polish underground outside the ghetto, he learned how to make Molotov cocktails. He brought this knowledge back to the ŻOB and helped organise their production in preparation for armed resistance.

This was particularly important for the ŻOB, which had only limited access to firearms. Molotov cocktails therefore became an important part of its preparations for the uprising.

When the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising began on 19 April 1943, Klepfisz fought in the area of the brushmakers’ workshops. He was killed on the second day of the uprising.

Klepfisz’s stone on the Hero’s Path commemorates both a fighter and the practical preparation for armed resistance the knowledge and networks that helped make the uprising possible.

media.credit: Photographer unknown, 31 July 1940. United States Holocaust Memorial Museum, via Wikimedia Commons. Public domain.
media.caption: Michał Klepfisz, Bund activist and member of the Jewish Combat Organization (ŻOB)

text.headline: Szmul Artur Zygielbojm  “Artur”
text.text:
Szmul "Artur" Zygielbojm, known underground as “Artur,” was a Bundist political leader and trade union activist.

Following the German occupation of Warsaw, Zygielbojm was ordered to serve on the Judenrat—the Jewish Council imposed by the German authorities to carry out their orders within the Jewish community. Its members were appointed rather than elected by the Jewish population. Zygielbojm resigned from the Judenrat after opposing German orders connected with the establishment of the Warsaw Ghetto.

After escaping occupied Poland, Zygielbojm eventually reached London, where he represented the Bund on the Polish National Council of the Polish government-in-exile. From there, he worked to bring reports of the mass murder of Polish Jews to the attention of Allied governments and the wider public.

On 12 May 1943, as the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising was being suppressed, Zygielbojm took his own life. In his final letter, he explained his decision as an act of protest against the failure of the world to intervene:

“I can neither be silent nor live when the last remnants of the Jewish people, whose representative I am, are being killed. My comrades in the Warsaw Ghetto have fallen with guns in their hands, in their last heroic struggle.”

He wrote that although he had not been able to die alongside them, he belonged with them, and hoped his death might provoke action to save Jews still alive.

Zygielbojm’s place on the Hero’s Path connects the uprising in Warsaw with the struggle beyond the ghetto to make the destruction of Polish Jewry known to the outside world.

media.credit: Photographer unknown, before 1939. Wikimedia Commons. Public domain
media.caption: Szmul Artur Zygielbojm, Bund activist and representative of the Jewish community in the Polish National Council in London.

text.headline: Izrael Chaim (Arie) Wilner  “Jurek”
text.text:
Izrael Chaim Wilner, also known as Arie Wilner and by his underground name “Jurek,” was a member of Hashomer Hatzair and one of the founders of the Jewish Fighting Organization (ŻOB).

Wilner served as an important link between the ŻOB and the Polish underground. Operating outside the ghetto, he maintained contacts with representatives of the Home Army (Armia Krajowa) and worked to obtain assistance and weapons for the Jewish resistance.

In March 1943, Wilner was arrested by the Gestapo and tortured. After escaping, he returned to the Warsaw Ghetto and took part in the uprising that began on 19 April.

For Wilner, armed resistance was also a question of how Jews would face their destruction. He expressed this in words remembered from the period:

“I do not want to remain alive and live a life of slavery and humiliation while most of my brothers are being annihilated. I want to die a hero’s death—a death with honor.”

Wilner was among those in the ŻOB command bunker at 18 Miła Street. On 8 May 1943, when the bunker was surrounded by German forces, he died there alongside Mordechaj Anielewicz and other ŻOB members.

Wilner’s place on the Hero’s Path commemorates both his role in building connections beyond the ghetto walls and his participation in armed resistance.

media.credit: Moreshet Mordechai Anielewicz Memorial, via United States Holocaust Memorial Museum
media.caption: Izrael Chaim (Arie) Wilner, known as “Jurek,” a founder and leader of the Jewish Combat Organization (ŻOB) and its liaison with the Polish underground

text.headline: Paweł Frenkiel Commander of the ŻZW
text.text:
Paweł Frenkiel was the commander of the Jewish Military Union (Żydowski Związek Wojskowy, ŻZW), one of the two principal Jewish armed resistance organisations that fought in the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising. A member of the Revisionist Zionist youth movement Betar, Frenkiel had served in the Polish Army and brought military experience to the organisation.

The ŻZW remained a separate organisation from the Jewish Fighting Organization (ŻOB) and entered the uprising substantially better armed. Although its main concentration of fighters was around Muranów Square, ŻZW units were positioned elsewhere in the ghetto, including close to ŻOB fighting positions.

When the uprising began on 19 April 1943, ŻZW fighters fought German forces from these positions. At Muranów Square they raised two flags above the ghetto—a Polish white-and-red flag and a blue-and-white Zionist flag. Visible beyond the ghetto walls, the flags became one of the most powerful symbols of the uprising.

Plans had been made before the uprising for groups of ŻZW fighters to leave the ghetto and continue the struggle outside Warsaw with partisan forces. During the fighting, Frenkiel and some members of the ŻZW left the ghetto as part of these plans, while other ŻZW fighters remained and continued fighting inside.

Frenkiel and members of his group continued their resistance outside the ghetto. Their location in Warsaw was eventually disclosed to the Germans, and Frenkiel and the ŻZW members with him were killed in the ensuing armed confrontation.

Other ŻZW members remained in the ghetto until its final liquidation and were deported with the remaining Jewish population. Some survived the camps and the war.

media.credit: Photograph by Mateusz Opasiński, 2012. Wikimedia Commons. CC BY-SA 3.0
media.caption: ero’s Path memorial stone commemorating Paweł Frenkiel and Dawid Moryc Apfelbaum, commanders associated with the Jewish Military Union (ŻZW).

text.headline: Mordechaj Anielewicz  Commander of the ŻOB
text.text:
Mordechaj Anielewicz was a member of the leadership of Hashomer Hatzair in the Warsaw Ghetto and became one of the leading figures in the organisation of armed Jewish resistance. He was one of the founders of the Jewish Fighting Organization (Żydowska Organizacja Bojowa, ŻOB) and became its commander.

When the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising began on 19 April 1943, Anielewicz led the ŻOB during the fighting.

In his final letter to Yitzhak Zuckerman, written during the uprising, Anielewicz reflected on what the fighters had achieved:

“The dream of my life has risen to become fact. Self-defense in the ghetto will have been a reality. Jewish armed resistance and revenge are facts.”

As German forces systematically burned the ghetto, Anielewicz and members of the ŻOB command moved to the bunker at 18 Miła Street. On 8 May 1943, German forces surrounded the bunker. Anielewicz died there alongside other ŻOB fighters.

Miła 18 would become closely associated with Anielewicz and the memory of the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising. But the construction of that memory began remarkably soon after the war.

media.credit: Photograph by Avraham Malavsky, 1936. Jewish National Fund (JNF) Photo Archive, file 037104. Public domain.
media.caption: Mordechaj Anielewicz, 1936. Anielewicz later became commander of the Jewish Combat Organization (ŻOB) during the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising.

text.headline: Miła 18 The 1946 Memorial
text.text:
On 19 April 1946, the third anniversary of the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising, survivors gathered at Miła 18 to commemorate the uprising. The memorial and commemorative stone were created by survivors, marking what was then believed to be the location of the ŻOB command bunker.

The commemoration took place only a year after the end of the war, while Warsaw still lay largely in ruins. At Miła 18, a mound was formed from the rubble of the destroyed ghetto, with a commemorative stone placed at its summit. The site was understood not only as the location of the bunker, but as a grave for those who had died there.

The dedication of the memorial in 1946 was the first commemorative act dedicated to the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising. Survivors themselves chose to mark this place and preserve its memory, establishing Miła 18 as a site of commemoration only three years after the uprising

media.credit: Archival film footage, Warsaw, 19 April 1946
media.caption: ommemoration at Miła 18 on 19 April 1946, the third anniversary of the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising. The memorial was erected by Jewish survivors amid the ruins of the former ghetto.

text.headline: Miła 18 Constructing Modern Memory
text.text:
The memorial created by survivors in 1946 remained at Miła 18, but the commemorative landscape surrounding it continued to develop.

In 2006, a new monument designed by Hanna Szmalenberg and Marek Moderau was unveiled at the foot of the mound. The monument incorporates the names of 51 fighters, while an inscription commemorates those who died in the bunker whose names remain unknown. The original mound and 1946 commemorative stone were retained, allowing different periods of remembrance to exist together within the same landscape.

Over time, Miła 18 has become one of the most recognisable sites associated with the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising. The landscape places particular emphasis on Mordechaj Anielewicz and the ŻOB, reinforcing their central position within the public memory of the uprising.

Yet only a short distance away, Paweł Frenkiel, commander of the ŻZW, is commemorated by a single stone on the Hero’s Path.

What determines which individuals, organisations and places become the symbols through which an historical event is remembered?

media.credit: Photograph by Dr. Avishai Teicher, 2013. Wikimedia Commons. CC BY-SA 3.0.
media.caption: The 2006 memorial at Miła 18, with the Anielewicz Mound behind it. The monument bears the names of 51 identified Jewish fighters.

text.headline: Miła 18 Archaeology and Memory
text.text:
In 2022, archaeological excavations began beside the Anielewicz Mound. Researchers uncovered the cellars of the pre-war buildings at Miła 18 and Miła 20 revealing physical traces of a landscape that had largely disappeared beneath post-war Warsaw.

At Miła 20, archaeologists discovered altered basement structures, including concrete walls, corridors and a reinforced room. The evidence suggests that these structures formed part of the extensive bunker complex traditionally associated with Miła 18. Thousands of objects were also recovered, including everyday items, books and religious objects belonging to Jewish residents of the area.

The excavations add another layer to the history of Miła 18. The site had already been commemorated for more than seventy-five years before archaeology began to reveal the physical remains beneath the memorial landscape.

What happens when archaeology adds new evidence to a place whose meaning has already been established through decades of commemoration and collective memory?

media.credit: Photograph by Miron Bogacki, 2022.
media.caption: Archaeological excavations near the Anielewicz Mound at Miła 18, summer 2022

text.headline: Meir Majerowicz “Marek” From Underground Press to Armed Resistance
text.text:
Meir Majerowicz, known as “Marek,” was a lawyer and a leading activist in Poale Zion–Right. In the Warsaw Ghetto, he was involved in the underground press and served as an editor of the clandestine Polish-language newspaper Nowe Tory.

Majerowicz also became involved in preparations for armed resistance. During the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising, he commanded a Poale Zion fighting group within the Jewish Fighting Organization (ŻOB).

After leaving the ghetto during the uprising, Majerowicz continued with members of the underground on the other side of Warsaw. He died in May 1943 in a fire at a photographic-film factory on 11 Listopada Street.

His story reflects the different forms resistance could take in the Warsaw Ghetto from clandestine political writing and communication to armed resistance.

media.credit: Image reproduced on POLIN GD, “Marek Majerowicz.” Original photographic source unknown
media.caption: Meir Majerowicz (“Marek”), commander of a Poale Zion combat group in the Jewish Combat Organization (ŻOB) during the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising.

text.headline: Frumka Płotnicka The Courier Girl
text.text:
Frumka Płotnicka was a member of the Dror Zionist youth movement and one of the kashariyot—the couriers who maintained connections between Jewish underground movements and communities across occupied Poland.

Women played a particularly important role as couriers. Travelling outside the ghettos under false identities, they crossed borders and checkpoints, carried messages, documents, money and underground publications, and transferred information between communities that had been deliberately isolated from one another. They also carried news of deportations and mass murder and helped connect developing resistance movements.

Płotnicka travelled extensively through occupied Poland. After the mass deportations from the Warsaw Ghetto in 1942, she went to Będzin, where she helped organise the Jewish underground and preparations for armed resistance.

On 17 July 1943, Płotnicka and other members of the underground wrote a final letter describing the destruction of Jewish communities across occupied Poland. Her words reflected what her work as a courier had allowed her to witness:

“I personally visited all the districts I have written about and witnessed all the acts of extermination.”

She also understood what the approaching liquidation of Będzin was likely to mean:

“When you receive this letter, none of us will be alive.”

And later:

“I doubt if you can help us in time, since we are nearing our final days.”

On 3 August 1943, during the final liquidation of the Będzin Ghetto, Płotnicka took part in the Będzin Ghetto Uprising. She was killed during the fighting.

media.credit: Ghetto Fighters’ House Archive, Photo Archive, catalogue no. 1262, registry no. 07035P. Donated by David Gottesforcht.
media.caption: Frumka Płotnicka, member of the Dror youth movement and liaison of the Jewish Combat Organization (ŻOB).

text.headline: Yitsḥak Nissenbaum Kiddush Ha-Hayyim
text.text:
Rabbi Yitsḥak Nissenbaum was a Zionist leader, writer and religious thinker who became an important figure in the Warsaw Ghetto. Before the war, he had been active in the Mizrachi religious Zionist movement, combining religious life with Zionist political and educational work.

In the ghetto, Nissenbaum continued to teach, write and provide religious and communal leadership. He is particularly associated with the concept of Kiddush Ha-Hayyim: the sanctification of life.

Jewish tradition had long spoken of Kiddush Ha-Shem (the sanctification of God’s name), including through martyrdom when Jews were forced to choose between abandoning their faith and death. Nissenbaum argued that under Nazi persecution the challenge was different. Jews were being targeted for destruction simply because they were Jews. In these circumstances, the imperative was to preserve Jewish life:

“This is a time for the sanctification of life, and not for the sanctification of the Name through death.”

Survival itself could therefore become an act of resistance: preserving Jewish life, community, belief and human dignity in circumstances designed to destroy them.

Yitsḥak Nissenbaum was murdered during the destruction of the Warsaw Ghetto in 1943.

media.credit: Abraham Schwadron Portrait Collection, National Library of Israel. Photograph taken in Warsaw, c. 1938; photographer unknown.
media.caption: Rabbi Yitsḥak Nissenbaum, religious-Zionist leader and president of the Mizrachi movement in Poland.

text.headline: Janusz Korczak and Stefania Wilczyńska Whose Name Becomes the Story?
text.text:
Janusz Korczak, physician, educator and writer, and Stefania Wilczyńska, educator and administrator, worked together for decades at the Jewish orphanage Dom Sierot in Warsaw. Wilczyńska was central to the daily running of the institution and to the development of its educational environment.

After the orphanage was forced into the Warsaw Ghetto, Korczak and Wilczyńska continued to care for the children under increasingly desperate conditions.

In August 1942, during the mass deportations from the Warsaw Ghetto, the children and staff of Dom Sierot were ordered to the Umschlagplatz. Korczak and Wilczyńska accompanied the children. They were deported together to Treblinka, where they were murdered.

Writing shortly afterwards, Warsaw Ghetto poet Władysław Szlengel described seeing Korczak accompany the children on their final journey:

“Today I saw Janusz Korczak,
As he walked with the children in the last procession.
And the children were in really clean clothes,
As if they were going in a walk in the gardens on Sunday …
Someone dashed up with a paper in his hand,
‘You can go back … there’s a card from Brandt.’
Korczak shook his head silently,
How could he get into those unfeeling heads
What it means to leave a child alone?”

Korczak became one of the most internationally recognised figures associated with the Holocaust and the fate of Jewish children. His decision to remain with the children has been commemorated in books, monuments, museums and educational institutions around the world.

Wilczyńska shared responsibility for the orphanage, remained with the children and shared their fate. Yet her name is far less prominent within public memory.

The Hero’s Path commemorates Janusz Korczak. It does not commemorate Stefania Wilczyńska.

Whose name becomes the story? What does this tell us about how individual figures come to represent a collective experience?

media.credit: Ghetto Fighters’ House Museum, Israel.
media.caption: Janusz Korczak and Stefania Wilczyńska at Gocławek, c. 1936.

text.headline: Yitsḥak Katzenelson Writing as Resistance
text.text:
Yitsḥak Katzenelson was a poet, playwright and educator who wrote in both Hebrew and Yiddish. After fleeing Łódź, he reached Warsaw and from 1940 lived in the Warsaw Ghetto.

In the ghetto, Katzenelson continued to write and teach. He participated in clandestine education, worked with youth movements and contributed his writings to the Ringelblum Archive. His poetry became a means of documenting and responding to the destruction taking place around him.

During the Great Deportation of 1942, Katzenelson’s wife and two of his sons were deported to Treblinka and murdered. Katzenelson remained in the ghetto with his surviving son, Zvi. On 20 April 1943, the day after the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising began, they were smuggled to the other side of Warsaw.

Katzenelson and Zvi eventually reached the Vittel internment camp in France. There, between October 1943 and January 1944, he wrote The Song of the Murdered Jewish People. In the opening section, Katzenelson calls upon the murdered to become present through his writing:

“Rise, show yourselves to me. Come all, come on,
I want to see you, want to look at you, want to contemplate
in silence my murdered people. And I’ll sing! Yes.”

The manuscript was hidden at Vittel and survived the war. Katzenelson and Zvi did not. In 1944, they were deported to Auschwitz-Birkenau, where they were murdered.

Katzenelson’s words survived to bear witness to people whose lives the Nazis sought to erase. His stone on the Hero’s Path places writing, testimony and remembrance alongside armed resistance as part of the memory of the Warsaw Ghetto.

media.credit: Schwadron Collection, National Library of Israel, 1908. Public domain.
media.caption: Yitsḥak Katzenelson, poet, teacher and author of The Song of the Murdered Jewish People.

text.headline: Umschlagplatz Deportation from the Warsaw Ghetto
text.text:
The Umschlagplatz at Stawki Street became the principal assembly and deportation point for Jews from the Warsaw Ghetto. From here, Jews were deported to extermination camps and forced-labour camps.

On 22 July 1942, the Germans began the Grossaktion Warschau, the mass deportation of the ghetto’s Jewish population. During the following two months, more than 260,000 Jews were deported to Treblinka, where they were murdered. Thousands more were murdered in the ghetto or deported to forced-labour camps.

People seized in round-ups or ordered from their homes were brought to the Umschlagplatz and held there before being forced into railway wagons. From this site, deportation trains carried Warsaw’s Jews away from the ghetto.

The site was first formally commemorated in 1948, when a sandstone plaque designed by architect Leon Marek Suzin was unveiled. The unveiling took place shortly before that of Nathan Rapoport’s Monument to the Ghetto Heroes, as participants proceeded from the Umschlagplatz toward the new monument.

In 1988, the earlier plaque was replaced by the monument we see today, designed by Hanna Szmalenberg and Władysław Klamerus, as part of the commemorative landscape that included the Hero’s Path. Its enclosed form evokes both the railway wagons used for deportation and the gateway through which deportees passed.

On its inner wall are 400 Jewish first names, representing the hundreds of thousands of individuals deported from Warsaw.

media.credit: Photograph: PAP, via Culture.pl.
media.caption: The Umschlagplatz Memorial at Stawki Street, Warsaw. Designed by Hanna Szmalenberg and Władysław Klamerus, the monument was unveiled in 1988.

text.headline: Jan Karski Carrying the Message
text.text:
Jan Karski, born Jan Kozielewski, was a courier and emissary for the Polish Underground State and the Polish government-in-exile. His missions carried information from occupied Poland to the Polish government and Allied leaders in the West.

In 1942, Jewish underground leaders arranged for Karski to enter the Warsaw Ghetto so that he could witness conditions there himself. He was also taken into Izbica, a transit ghetto through which Jews were being deported to the Bełżec extermination camp. What he witnessed became part of the information he carried out of occupied Poland.

Karski reached London, where he reported to the Polish government-in-exile and British officials, including Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden. He later travelled to the United States, where he met President Franklin D. Roosevelt in July 1943.

Decades later, Karski himself became part of the commemorative landscape of the former Warsaw Ghetto. The Jan Karski bench, designed by sculptor Karol Badyna, was unveiled here on 11 June 2013. The monument was proposed by the Museum of Polish History and financed by the City of Warsaw, adding another twenty-first-century layer to the continually developing landscape of memory surrounding the former ghetto.

media.credit: photograph by Lynne Feldman, Warsaw, 2026
media.caption: The Jan Karski Bench in Warsaw, created by sculptor Karol Badyna and unveiled in 2013

text.headline: The First Monument 1947
text.text:
In 1947, a memorial designed by architect Leon Marek Suzin was erected on the ruins of the Warsaw Ghetto, close to the location of one of the ghetto’s main gates.

The monument consists of two distinct but connected sections. The first is a flat circular plaque embedded in the ground, bearing a bronze palm branch and the Hebrew letter Bet (ב). The palm branch symbolises martyrdom, while Bet, the first letter of the Book of Genesis, represents Bereshit — “In the beginning.”

Beyond it, three steps lead to a raised semicircular platform. At its centre is another circular disc, bearing an inscription in Polish, Hebrew and Yiddish. Its position and elevation point toward the location of the now-absent ghetto gate, connecting the memorial directly to the landscape of the former ghetto.

The inscription reads:

“To those who fell in the unprecedented heroic battle for the dignity and freedom of the Jewish people, for a free Poland and for a man’s liberation. The Polish Jews.”

Created only two years after the end of the war, the monument provides an early example of how the Warsaw Ghetto was commemorated in the landscape. Its language is particularly significant: Jewish resistance, Polish freedom and universal human liberation are brought together within the same act of remembrance.

media.credit: Photograph by Lynne Feldman, Warsaw, 2026.
media.caption: The first Monument to the Ghetto Heroes, designed by Leon Marek Suzin and unveiled in 1946.

text.headline: Żegota Remembering Rescue
text.text:
The Council to Aid Jews, Żegota, was established in December 1942 as part of the underground structures of the Polish Government-in-Exile. Working in German-occupied Poland, its members provided assistance to Jews in hiding, including false documents, financial support, accommodation and help for children.

Żegota brought together people from different political and social backgrounds, both Jewish and non-Jewish, working through clandestine networks at enormous personal risk. Among those associated with its work were Zofia Kossak-Szczucka, Władysław Bartoszewski, Adolf Berman and Irena Sendler.

In 1995, a memorial to Żegota was unveiled close to the Monument to the Ghetto Heroes. Initiated by Władysław Bartoszewski and designed by Hanna Szmalenberg and Marek Moderau, the monument added another layer to the developing commemorative landscape of the former Warsaw Ghetto.

Its presence here brings the story of organised efforts to rescue Jews under German occupation into a landscape already shaped by the memory of Jewish persecution and resistance

media.credit: POLIN Museum of the History of Polish Jews / Polish Righteous portal.
media.caption: The Żegota Memorial, commemorating the Council to Aid Jews. Designed by Hanna Szmalenberg and Marek Moderau and unveiled in 1995

text.headline: Monument to the Ghetto Heroes 1948
text.text:
On 19 April 1948, the fifth anniversary of the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising, the Monument to the Ghetto Heroes was unveiled on the ruins of the former ghetto. Created by sculptor Nathan Rapoport, with the architectural design by Leon Marek Suzin, the monument gave the uprising a monumental presence within the landscape of post-war Warsaw.

The granite wall supporting the monument evokes both the walls of the Warsaw Ghetto and the Western Wall in Jerusalem, connecting the destroyed ghetto with Jewish history, destruction and enduring memory.

The monument presents two contrasting representations of Jewish experience. On the western side, seven monumental figures emerge from flames. Men and women are depicted together as heroic fighters, almost all carrying weapons. At the centre stands a symbolic representation of Mordechaj Anielewicz, holding a grenade. References to earlier traditions of heroic representation—including the fallen soldier and the female figure recalling revolutionary imagery—place the Warsaw Ghetto fighters within a broader visual language of heroism.

The eastern side presents a very different image. Twelve figures, recalling the twelve tribes of Israel, are huddled together with their eyes lowered. Only the figure of a rabbi, holding a Torah scroll, looks upward. The relief evokes the exile of the Jewish people following the destruction of the Second Temple, connecting the deportation and destruction of Warsaw Jewry with a much longer history of Jewish suffering and displacement.

At the base of the monument, constructed partly with rubble from Muranów, four menorot provide further references to Jewish history and memory, including the Temple and the Maccabees.

Rapoport later recalled the unveiling:

“As we stood on the ashes of the Ghetto, fragments of burned pages of Jewish prayer books fluttered in the air around us; a profound silence prevailed. On a temporary altar the Rabbi chanted mournful prayers for the martyrs. The menorah on the monument were aglow with flames. People were crying.”

He also explained the thinking behind the monument:

“One can imagine how difficult it was to plan a work of such emotional impact. The site in Warsaw was wilderness; therefore, I decided to build a wall as a support and as a symbol of the vanished ghetto. The front relief in bronze is dedicated to the uprising; the rear in granite represents the deportation.”

Since its unveiling in 1948, the monument has become one of the defining images through which the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising has been remembered. Yet, as the path we have followed demonstrates, the landscape around it has never stopped changing.

The Hero’s Path is therefore not simply a route through the history of the Warsaw Ghetto. It is a route through the construction of its memory.

Who and what has been chosen for commemoration? Who is absent? And how have those choices shaped the way we remember the Warsaw Ghetto today?

Source: James E. Young, “The Biography of a Memorial Icon: Nathan Rapoport’s Warsaw Ghetto Monument,” Representations, no. 26 (1989): 82–90.
